title: 02. Python
description: Python fundamentals for the Turing MCQ screen and Andela HackerRank challenge: data types, collections, comprehensions, OOP, decorators, generators, async/await, the GIL, and common standard library patterns.

02.1 Core Types & Mutability: Mutable: list, dict, set, bytearray. Immutable: tuple, str, int, float, frozenset, bytes.
Default mutable argument bug: `def fn(x=[])` reuses the same list across calls. Fix: `def fn(x=None): x = x or []`.
String interning: small integers and short strings are cached — `a is b` can be True even without `==`.
f-strings (3.6+): fastest string formatting. `f'{value:.2f}'` for formatting.
Walrus operator `:=` (3.8+): assign inside expression — `while chunk := f.read(8192):`.
02.2 Collections: list: O(1) append/pop-end, O(n) insert/search. Backed by dynamic array.
dict: O(1) average get/set (hash table). Ordered by insertion in 3.7+.
set: O(1) average add/remove/contains. Unordered, no duplicates.
collections.deque: O(1) append/pop from both ends. Better than list for queue.
collections.Counter: count hashable elements. `.most_common(n)` returns top n.
collections.defaultdict: dict with default factory — no KeyError on missing key.
02.3 Comprehensions & Generators: List comp: `[x*2 for x in range(10) if x%2==0]` — eager, loads all into memory.
Generator expr: `(x*2 for x in range(10))` — lazy, one item at a time. Use for large datasets.
dict comp: `{k: v for k, v in items.items()}`. set comp: `{x for x in lst}`.
yield: turns a function into a generator. `yield from` delegates to sub-generator.
Generators can't be rewound — once exhausted, they're done.
02.4 OOP: `@classmethod`: receives `cls` — alternative constructors. `@staticmethod`: no implicit args.
MRO (Method Resolution Order): C3 linearisation. `ClassName.__mro__` shows the lookup order.
02.5 Decorators, GIL, Async: Decorator: function that wraps another function. `@functools.wraps(fn)` preserves the wrapped function's metadata.
GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): CPython only allows one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads work for I/O-bound tasks; use `multiprocessing` for CPU-bound.
`asyncio`: cooperative multitasking. `async def` + `await` — single thread, yields at I/O points. Not parallelism.
`concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`: easy thread pool for I/O-bound work.
Type hints (3.5+): `def fn(x: int) -> str`. `Optional[str]` = `str | None` (3.10+: `str | None`).

questions.prompt:
What is the output of this code?
```python
def append_to(x, lst=[]):
    lst.append(x)
    return lst

print(append_to(1))
print(append_to(2))
```

options.text: [1] then [2]
[] then []
Error — default args can't be lists

questions.explanation: Mutable default argument trap: `lst=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, not each call. The same list object is reused across all calls without an explicit `lst` argument. After call 1: lst=[1]. After call 2: lst=[1,2]. Fix: `def append_to(x, lst=None): lst = [] if lst is None else lst`.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `is` and `==` in Python?

options.text: They are interchangeable
`is` checks identity (same object in memory); `==` checks equality (same value via `__eq__`)
`is` is faster but only works for strings
`==` compares references; `is` compares values

questions.explanation: `a is b` → `id(a) == id(b)` → same object. `a == b` → `a.__eq__(b)` → same value. Pitfall: `[] == []` is True; `[] is []` is False (different objects). Small integer caching (-5 to 256) means `a = 256; b = 256; a is b` can be True — but don't rely on this. Always use `==` for value comparison; use `is` only for `None` checks: `if x is None`.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a tuple over a list in Python?

options.text: Always — tuples are faster for all operations
When the data is heterogeneous and shouldn't change (coordinates, RGB values, DB row) — immutability signals intent and allows use as dict keys / set elements
When you need to sort the collection
Tuples are only for return values from functions

questions.explanation: Tuple = immutable sequence. Use for: data that logically shouldn't be modified (`(lat, lon)`, `(name, age)`), dict keys (`{(0,0): 'origin'}`), multiple return values (`return x, y`). List = mutable sequence. Use for: homogeneous collections that grow/shrink. Tuples have slightly lower memory overhead and can be used as dict keys/set elements (because they're hashable, assuming their elements are too).

questions.prompt: Which string formatting method is preferred in modern Python (3.6+) and why?

options.text: `'Hello %s' % name` — classic and most compatible
`f'Hello {name}'` — f-strings: fastest at runtime, most readable, supports expressions
`'Hello {}'.format(name)` — most explicit
`'Hello ' + name` — concatenation is clearest

questions.explanation: F-strings (3.6+) are evaluated at runtime, compiled to efficient bytecode, and the fastest formatting method. They support any expression: `f'{2+2}'`, `f'{obj.method()}'`, `f'{value:.2f}'`. They're also the most readable — no placeholder mismatch possible. `%` and `.format()` are older patterns. String concatenation with `+` in a loop is O(n²) — use `''.join(parts)` instead.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of `list.insert(0, x)` in Python?

options.text: O(1) — Python lists are linked lists
O(n) — all elements after the insert point must be shifted right
O(log n) — Python uses a balanced tree
O(1) amortised — same as append

questions.explanation: Python lists are backed by a dynamic array. `append` = O(1) amortised (occasional resize). `insert(0, x)` = O(n) because all n existing elements are shifted one position right. `pop()` (end) = O(1). `pop(0)` (front) = O(n). For O(1) front operations, use `collections.deque`: `deque.appendleft(x)` = O(1).

questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity for `x in my_set` vs `x in my_list` in Python?

options.text: Both O(1)
set: O(1) average; list: O(n) — set uses hash table, list does linear scan
Both O(n)
set: O(log n); list: O(1)

questions.explanation: `set` (hash table): `in` is O(1) average, O(n) worst case (hash collision). `list`: `in` is O(n) linear scan. For frequent membership checks on large collections, always convert to a set: `lookup = set(my_list)`. This is a classic Python interview trap — checking `x in list` inside a loop gives O(n²) when O(n) is achievable with a set.

questions.prompt: What does `collections.Counter('aabbbcc').most_common(2)` return?
questions.explanation: `Counter` counts hashable elements. `Counter('aabbbcc')` = `{'a':2, 'b':3, 'c':2}`. `.most_common(2)` returns a list of (element, count) tuples sorted by count descending: `[('b', 3), ('a', 2)]`. Useful for: frequency problems (LeetCode 347 Top K Frequent), anagram checks (`Counter(s) == Counter(t)`), word frequency counts.

questions.prompt: When does `collections.defaultdict(list)` save you code compared to a plain `dict`?

options.text: When you need a sorted dictionary
When grouping items by key — avoids manually checking `if key not in d: d[key] = []` before appending
When you need O(1) lookup
`defaultdict` is slower so you should always use plain `dict`

questions.explanation: Without defaultdict: `if word not in groups: groups[word] = []; groups[word].append(doc)`. With `defaultdict(list)`: `groups[word].append(doc)` — missing key auto-initialises to `[]`. Common patterns: `defaultdict(list)` for grouping, `defaultdict(int)` for counting (alternative to Counter), `defaultdict(set)` for adjacency lists in graphs. `dict.setdefault(key, [])` is the plain-dict equivalent.

questions.prompt: You need a queue (FIFO) in Python. Why is `collections.deque` better than `list` for this?

options.text: deque supports more methods than list
`deque.popleft()` is O(1); `list.pop(0)` is O(n) — deque uses a doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks
deque is thread-safe by default
list doesn't support FIFO — you must use deque

questions.explanation: `list.pop(0)` shifts all remaining elements left — O(n). `deque.popleft()` = O(1) because deque is implemented as a doubly-linked list of fixed blocks. For BFS, sliding window, or any queue: use `deque`. `deque.append` (right) and `deque.appendleft` (left) are both O(1). Note: `deque` with `maxlen` parameter auto-discards old items — useful for rolling windows.

questions.prompt: You have a file with 10 million lines. What's the memory-efficient way to process them?

options.text: `lines = [line for line in f]` — load all into a list then process
`for line in f:` or a generator expression `(process(line) for line in f)` — reads one line at a time
`lines = f.readlines()` — readlines is optimised for large files
Split the file into 10 chunks and process in parallel

questions.explanation: File objects in Python are iterators — iterating `for line in f:` reads one line at a time without loading the whole file. `readlines()` loads everything into a list — ~1GB for a 10M-line file. Generator expression: `total = sum(len(line) for line in f)` processes lazily. Rule: if you don't need all items simultaneously, use a generator. Use list comprehension only when you need random access or multiple passes.

questions.prompt: What does `yield` do to a function?

options.text: It returns a value and ends the function, like return
It turns the function into a generator — calling it returns a generator object; the function body runs lazily, pausing at each `yield` and resuming on `next()`
It pauses execution for one second (async sleep)
`yield` is the same as `await` in async functions

questions.explanation: Generator function: contains `yield`. Calling it returns a generator object (no code runs yet). `next(gen)` runs until the next `yield`, returns the yielded value, and suspends. On the next `next()`, execution resumes from after `yield`. `StopIteration` is raised when the function returns. Memory efficient: only one value in memory at a time. `yield from iterable` delegates to a sub-generator.

questions.prompt: What does `[x for row in matrix for x in row]` do?

options.text: Creates a list of lists
Flattens a 2D list (matrix) into a 1D list — iterates outer then inner
Transposes the matrix
Raises a SyntaxError — nested comprehensions require parentheses

questions.explanation: Nested comprehension reads left-to-right like nested for loops: `for row in matrix:` (outer) then `for x in row:` (inner). Result: all elements from all rows in one flat list. `[[1,2],[3,4]] → [1,2,3,4]`. Note: the order of `for` clauses matches the order of nested `for` loops. `[[x for x in row] for row in matrix]` = copy of the matrix (list of lists).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `@classmethod` and `@staticmethod`?

options.text: They are identical — different syntactic sugar
`@classmethod` receives `cls` (the class) as the first argument — used for alternative constructors. `@staticmethod` receives no implicit argument — it's a plain function namespaced inside the class.
`@staticmethod` receives `self`; `@classmethod` receives nothing
Both receive `self` — the difference is that `@classmethod` can access class-level attributes

questions.explanation: `@classmethod`: `def from_string(cls, s): return cls(...)` — receives the class, can create instances of subclasses correctly (polymorphic factory). `@staticmethod`: `def validate(x): ...` — no `self` or `cls`, can't access instance or class state. Use classmethod for: alternative constructors, factory methods. Use staticmethod for: utility functions logically grouped with the class but not needing its state.

questions.prompt: You want instances of your `Money` class to be usable as dict keys and in sets. Which dunder methods must you implement?

options.text: `__str__` and `__repr__`
`__eq__` and `__hash__` — both required; if you define `__eq__`, Python sets `__hash__ = None` by default, making the object unhashable
No special methods needed — all Python objects are hashable

questions.explanation: For hashable objects (dict keys, set members): must implement both `__eq__` and `__hash__`. Constraint: if `a == b` then `hash(a) == hash(b)`. If you define `__eq__` without `__hash__`, Python 3 sets `__hash__ = None` — the object becomes unhashable. `@dataclass(frozen=True)` auto-generates both. `@dataclass` without `frozen` only generates `__eq__` (not `__hash__`).

questions.prompt: Class `C(A, B)` — both A and B define `method()`. Which version gets called when `C().method()` is invoked?

options.text: B's method — rightmost parent wins
A's method — Python's MRO (C3 linearisation) checks left to right: C → A → B → object
An error — multiple inheritance with overlapping methods raises TypeError
The most recently defined method wins

questions.explanation: MRO (Method Resolution Order): C3 linearisation. For `class C(A, B)`: search order is C → A → B → object. Left-to-right, depth-first. Check with `C.__mro__`. `super()` follows MRO — useful for cooperative multiple inheritance. Diamond problem is resolved by MRO — each class appears exactly once. `super().method()` in A calls B's version next (not object's).

questions.prompt: What does `@dataclass` auto-generate for a class?

options.text: Only `__init__`
`__init__` (from annotated fields), `__repr__`, and `__eq__` by default. With `frozen=True`: also `__hash__`. With `order=True`: `__lt__`, `__le__`, etc.
All dunder methods
`@dataclass` is only for immutable data — it always freezes the class

questions.explanation: `@dataclass` reads class-level type annotations as fields and generates boilerplate. `field(default_factory=list)` for mutable defaults. `frozen=True` makes instances immutable and adds `__hash__`. `slots=True` (3.10+) uses `__slots__` for memory efficiency. Preferred over `NamedTuple` when you need mutability or inheritance. NamedTuple: immutable, works as tuple (indexable, unpackable).

questions.prompt: What does a decorator do in Python?

options.text: Adds type annotations to a function
Wraps a function with another function — takes the original function as input, returns a new function that adds behaviour before/after the original
Compiles Python to bytecode for speed
Makes a function a class method

questions.explanation: `@timer` above `def fn():` is syntactic sugar for `fn = timer(fn)`. The decorator receives `fn`, creates a `wrapper` that adds behaviour (logging, timing, auth), calls `fn`, returns the result. `@functools.wraps(fn)` on the wrapper preserves `fn.__name__`, `fn.__doc__`. Common decorators: `@property`, `@staticmethod`, `@classmethod`, `@lru_cache`, `@retry`.

questions.prompt: When is `@functools.lru_cache` appropriate and what's its key requirement?

options.text: For any function — caching is always a win
For pure functions with hashable arguments — the function must return the same output for the same inputs (no side effects), and all arguments must be hashable
Only for recursive functions — it doesn't work for regular functions
`lru_cache` is deprecated in Python 3.9+

questions.explanation: `@lru_cache(maxsize=128)` memoises calls: first call computes and caches; same args → cached result. Requirements: (1) Pure function — same args must always produce same output. (2) Hashable args — can't cache calls with list/dict arguments (raise TypeError). Use `maxsize=None` for unlimited cache (equivalent to `@cache` in 3.9+). Great for: recursive DP (Fibonacci, coin change), expensive API lookups with repeated calls.

questions.prompt: You have a CPU-bound Python function. Will using `threading.Thread` make it run faster on a multi-core machine? Why?

options.text: Yes — threading always uses multiple cores
No — CPython's GIL prevents multiple threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously. CPU-bound threads time-slice on one core. Use `multiprocessing` for true CPU parallelism.
Yes — the GIL is released for CPU-bound operations
No — Python doesn't support threads at all

questions.explanation: GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): CPython holds a lock per Python process — only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. For CPU-bound work: threads don't speed things up (just context-switch on one core). The GIL IS released for: I/O operations, NumPy C extensions, and other C extensions that explicitly release it. Solutions for CPU-bound: `multiprocessing` (separate processes, each with own GIL), `concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor`, or PyPy (no GIL).

questions.prompt: When should you use `asyncio` instead of `threading` for I/O-bound work?

options.text: asyncio is always faster — always prefer it
asyncio: when you control the code end-to-end and can use async libraries (aiohttp, asyncpg). Threading: when using blocking libraries you can't change or when concurrency count is small (< 50).
They are identical for I/O-bound work — choose either
asyncio requires multiple cores to be effective

questions.explanation: asyncio: cooperative multitasking — single thread, explicit yield at `await`. Excellent for: thousands of concurrent I/O ops (HTTP requests, DB queries). But: entire call chain must be async — can't `await` inside a sync function. threading: preemptive — OS switches threads. Works with blocking libraries. Limit: OS thread overhead caps at ~1000 threads. Hybrid: `asyncio.run_in_executor` runs blocking functions in a thread pool from async code.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call an `async def` function without `await`?

options.text: The function runs synchronously
It returns a coroutine object — the function body hasn't run yet. You must `await` it or use `asyncio.run()` to execute it.
A RuntimeError is raised immediately
Python automatically awaits it

questions.explanation: `async def fn():` defines a coroutine function. Calling `fn()` returns a coroutine object — no code inside runs. You must: (1) `await fn()` from another async function; (2) `asyncio.run(fn())` from sync code; or (3) `asyncio.create_task(fn())` to schedule concurrently. Python warns about `RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited` if you forget. This is the most common async beginner mistake.

questions.prompt: Which `itertools` function efficiently generates all pairs from two lists without nested loops?

options.text: `itertools.chain(a, b)` — concatenates iterables
`itertools.product(a, b)` — Cartesian product, equivalent to nested for loops
`itertools.zip_longest(a, b)` — zips with fill value
`itertools.combinations(a, 2)` — pairs from a single iterable

questions.explanation: `itertools.product([1,2], ['a','b'])` yields `(1,'a'), (1,'b'), (2,'a'), (2,'b')` — Cartesian product. Memory efficient: lazy. Also useful: `combinations(lst, r)` = r-length combos without repetition; `permutations(lst, r)` = with order; `chain(a, b)` = concatenate iterators; `groupby(sorted_lst, key)` = SQL-style group-by; `islice(iter, n)` = take first n from iterator.

questions.prompt: What is a context manager (`with` statement) and why use it?

options.text: A threading primitive for locking shared resources
An object that defines `__enter__` and `__exit__` — guarantees cleanup (close file, release lock) even if an exception occurs inside the `with` block
A decorator for async functions
A way to define module-level constants

questions.explanation: `with open('file') as f:` — `f.__enter__()` called on entry, `f.__exit__()` called on exit even if an exception occurs. This ensures files are closed, DB connections released, locks freed. Custom: implement `__enter__` and `__exit__`, or use `@contextlib.contextmanager` with `yield`. `contextmanager` pattern: setup before `yield`, cleanup after `yield` (in `finally`).

questions.prompt: How do you sort a list of dicts by multiple keys — first by 'age' descending, then by 'name' ascending?

options.text: `sorted(lst, key=lambda x: (x['age'], x['name']), reverse=True)` — single reverse applies to both
`sorted(lst, key=lambda x: (-x['age'], x['name']))` — negate numeric key to reverse; string can't be negated, so sort ascending naturally
`lst.sort(by=['age', 'name'], ascending=[False, True])` — pandas-style
Python doesn't support multi-key sorting

questions.explanation: Python's sort is stable — sort by secondary key first, then primary. Or in one pass: return a tuple key. For descending numeric: negate it (`-x['age']`). For descending string: can't negate, but `(x['age'] * -1, x['name'])` works when age is the primary. Alternative: `functools.cmp_to_key` for complex comparisons. `sorted()` returns new list; `list.sort()` sorts in place.

questions.prompt: Which Pythonic idiom replaces `for i in range(len(lst)): print(i, lst[i])`?

options.text: `for i, val in enumerate(lst): print(i, val)` — returns (index, value) pairs
`for val in zip(range(len(lst)), lst): print(val)`
`for val in lst.items(): print(val)` — `.items()` works on lists
`for i, val in lst: print(i, val)`

questions.explanation: `enumerate(lst)` yields `(0, lst[0]), (1, lst[1]), ...`. Pythonic, avoids manual indexing, works with any iterable. `enumerate(lst, start=1)` starts from 1. `zip(a, b)` pairs elements from two iterables — use for parallel iteration. `zip(*matrix)` transposes a 2D list. `zip_longest(a, b, fillvalue=None)` handles iterables of different lengths.

questions.prompt: What does the walrus operator `:=` (Python 3.8+) allow?

options.text: Assignment inside an expression — avoids recomputing values in loops and comprehensions
Dictionary merging — same as `{**a, **b}`
In-place addition — shorthand for `+=`
Structural pattern matching

questions.explanation: `:=` (walrus / assignment expression): `while chunk := file.read(8192):` — reads chunk and checks truthiness in one expression without calling `read()` twice. In comprehensions: `filtered = [y := transform(x), y*2]` — compute `transform(x)` once and use the result multiple times. Use sparingly — overuse hurts readability. Useful for: while loops avoiding double calls, filtering and using computed values in the same comprehension.

questions.prompt: What does `__slots__` do in a Python class and when should you use it?

options.text: It defines which methods the class exposes
Declares fixed instance attributes — prevents `__dict__` creation, reducing memory by 40-60% per instance. Use when creating millions of small instances.
It's a hook for the `with` statement
`__slots__` makes attributes read-only

questions.explanation: By default, instances store attributes in a `__dict__` (hash table overhead per object). `__slots__ = ('x', 'y')`: replaces `__dict__` with fixed C-level slots — ~40-60% less memory per instance. Tradeoffs: can't add dynamic attributes, multiple inheritance with slots has caveats. Use for: data-heavy classes (millions of points, game entities). `@dataclass(slots=True)` (3.10+) adds slots automatically.

questions.prompt: Which standard library modules are most commonly useful in coding challenges? (select all)

options.text: `heapq` — min-heap (priority queue) in O(log n)
`bisect` — binary search on sorted lists
`re` — regular expressions
`collections` — Counter, deque, defaultdict, OrderedDict
`tkinter` — GUI toolkit for challenge problems

questions.explanation: E is wrong — tkinter is a GUI library, not useful in algorithm challenges. A: `heapq.heappush/heappop` for priority queues (Dijkstra, k-th largest). B: `bisect.bisect_left(sorted_list, x)` — O(log n) insertion point. C: `re.findall`, `re.sub` for string manipulation problems. D: `Counter` for frequencies, `deque` for BFS/sliding window, `defaultdict` for grouping. Also: `math.gcd`, `math.inf`, `functools.lru_cache`.
